Thank you Terence & SAIR team, I really enjoyed this..

One unexpected outcome for me was transferring some of the Stage 2 learnings to the Lean Kernel Arena, where our Lean kernel subsequently reached #1 and is currently ~18× faster than the official Lean checker. We've only just started applying the learnings there and elsewhere, so the cross-benchmark transfer is particularly interesting.

Would definitely love to participate again and looking forward to future challenges.
messages.subject: Sharing thoughts and experiences

messages.content:
Terence Tao said:

Thanks to everyone who participated in the Math Distillation Challenge! We hope to run final evaluations and publish the results soon.

In the meantime, I'd like to open this thread for people to share their experiences in this competition, and give any feedback on how to improve the experience for future competitions.

Thank you for running this challenge. What made the challenge attractive for me was the Lean judge with a plain accept/reject, the public reference pipeline that runs locally, the two tracks, and the freedom to submit any program at all. And I enjoyed learning more about universal algebra.

My main observation concerns the "distillation" question itself. I built a single-file solver with no lookup tables and no precomputed proofs.
It scored 200/200 on the held-out stress set in both tracks, with no wrong verdict across more than 3 000 judged problems, and it did so without the LLM.
I measured the LLM stage at the official settings: it never decided a verdict the deterministic part could
not reach on its own, prompt variants made no measurable difference, and on the stress set it was never invoked.
I see this as a genuine result of the competition rather than a failure: it shows where a text-completing model adds no value, and therefore where a next round could look. Two setup choices amplified it. The model sits at the end of the pipeline, called by a Python program to emit Lean text in one shot, and it runs at low reasoning effort with a fixed seed, so it can neither explore nor learn within a problem.

As an alternative setup, the model could lead instead of serve: the LLM would be the agent, and the submission its scaffold, with a Lean REPL and a Python sandbox as tools. I did not try it right now. But basically this is a setup for agentic coding tools use in software development. The judge plays the role of the compiler and test suite, and the scaffold is exactly the distilled artifact the competition was asking for.

I am looking forward to the forthcoming Lean kernel challenge.
